turns.reply:
Cart grease and wet stone. The road slopes down toward the gate through a press of morning traffic — a drover's cart, geese in wicker, two women with firewood bundles arguing about a debt in low, tired voices that have clearly been going on for years.

Ashbridge's wall runs gray and patched across the road, older than the city it guards, thicker at the base where the mortar has been rebuilt five different ways in five different centuries. A watch-tower stands at each shoulder. On the nearer one, a banner hangs limp in the windless stretch of morning — dark field, some emblem the distance flattens.

The queue for the west gate is short this early. Ahead of Alaric, a carter with a load of turnips is already in loud negotiation with a gate sergeant whose expression says he has heard every version of this conversation since before the carter owned a cart.

"—told you Tuesday, didn't I? Market-day toll's the same for turnips as it is for silk, Muller, I don't set it—"

"The Guild sets it. The Guild eats off my back is what it—"

"Then take it up with the Guild." The sergeant — chain shirt under a faded blue tabard, crossbow slung and clearly ornamental at this hour — waves the cart through without waiting for the argument to finish. His eye is already on the next in line, moving down the queue with the flat efficiency of a man counting heads and purses at the same time. Wood-bundles women. A boy with a hand-barrow of river eels. Then Alaric.

The sergeant's gaze does the usual pass — face, bow, quiver, the light armor under the travel clothes — and settles, briefly, on the red eyes. Whatever he makes of them, he doesn't make it aloud.

"Two coppers entry, stranger. Weapons stay slung inside the walls." He holds out a flat palm, weathered and cracked at the knuckles, and behind him the gate tunnel breathes cold air and the smell of the river. "Business in Ashbridge?"

"Silver." The sergeant bites it out of habit, thumb along the edge, then digs a coin purse off his belt. "Two coppers the toll. Count's eight back." Eight coppers drop into Alaric's palm one at a time, counted aloud in a voice worn down to gravel — "three, four, five — there, eight. Gate's yours."

Behind him the eel-barrow boy mutters something about strangers who can't count change, and the sergeant ignores him the way a man ignores weather.

"Guild?" He jerks his chin through the tunnel, where the cold and the river smell come off the stone. "Straight through, keep left at the fountain square — the big one, not the well lane. Cross the high bridge, river street runs you right to it. Stone hall with the crossed swords over the door. Big sign. Can't miss it, they pay the city good money so nobody can." He steps aside, waving the firewood women forward, done with Alaric as thoroughly as a door closing. "Next. Two coppers."

The gate tunnel swallows sound as anyone walks in — cartwheels and voices coming back off the stone doubled, the drover's turnip cart somewhere ahead still rolling, Muller's voice lost in the echo. Daylight shows at the far end, a slice of it, rooftops and chimney smoke beyond.

"—half the bounty is half the bounty, Drem, it's arithmetic—"

"Arithmetic? You took the throw. I took the *tusk*. Where in Duskreach's name do you figure the tusk sits on a boar, Hesta, the tail?"

Two adventurers at the notice board, a boar's severed tusk actually on the counter between them, still fly-crusted. Nobody in the hall looks up. Morning in the Ashbridge Guild runs on this fuel.

The hall itself is old timber and river stone, beams dark with decades of pipe smoke, crossed swords riveted over a door tall enough for a mounted man. Rain lamps burn along the rafters even in daylight — river fogs reach this far up the street. Benches line the walls, most full: a sleeping man with his boots on a table, a pair of women cleaning rust off chainmail with sand and rags, a courier slumped over a mug he's clearly treating as medicine.

Behind the long counter, a woman with iron-gray hair braided crownwise is already writing before anyone reaches her, ink to the second knuckle.

"Board's posted, contracts are numbered, don't pull a slip unless you mean to run it." Then she looks up. The pen stops. "Ah. New face. Bow, light kit, gate-fresh dust." The pen taps the counter twice. "You'll be wanting the desk, then. I'm Ferran. Registrations, payouts, and everything the board doesn't say out loud."

She hauls a ledger over, licks her thumb, finds the page.

"Before anything — I need to know if you've done this before. Any guild, any city. Blackgate registry, mercenary company, even a caravan charter counts." Her eyes go once to the red eyes and come back down to the ledger without a word spent on them, the way a woman counts a loose rail on a bridge and keeps walking. "Because it changes what I write. Green hands get a sponsor clause. Trained hands get the standard oath and a board key."

From the bench by the door, the boar argument arrives at the counter without either party apparently deciding to move it there. The tusk lands with a knock.

Hesta — broad, sunburnt, one ear notched like a steer's — plants both fists. "Ferran. Tell this man a tusk is a trophy portion."

Ferran doesn't look up from her ledger. "Drem threw first, the split was posted at three-two before you left, Hesta. I have it in ink. You signed the ink."

"I signed it *tired*—"

"Signatures don't get tired." Ferran's pen finally lifts, and she aims it at Drem. "Pay the woman her three-tenths and stop feeding my morning." Then, back to Alaric, the ledger turned flat on the counter, a blank registration form and a small pot of ink slid alongside it. A quill, goose-feather, chewed at the top.

"So. Trained or green? And a name for the book — your own, mind, whatever else about you stays your own business."

Behind the counter, Drem is counting coppers onto the wood one at a time, loudly, each coin placed like an insult.

The last copper goes down under Drem's finger with a click, placed like the coin personally wronged him. Hesta rakes the pile into her belt-pouch without a word of thanks and Drem mutters something about robbery with paperwork, and the two of them drift a step down the counter — not leaving, evidently. Watching. A hall this size, a new face is the morning's entertainment.

Ferran's pen moves before the bow finishes. "Alaric. No family. First branch." She says it the way she'd read a delivery list. "That's green, then, and green changes the paper."

She pulls a second form from the drawer, lays it beside the first, and squares the corners so both line up exact.

"Green hands run their first three contracts under a sponsor's mark. Rank D or better. They sign next to you on every slip, and if you don't come back, the loss goes in their column. It's not sentiment. It's arithmetic." The pen taps the counter twice. "Green hands die on their first contract more often than the contract's quarry does. The clause exists because I have buried it. That's all anyone needs to hear on the matter."

The sleeping man on the bench snorts without waking. Ferran ignores him.

"Oath you can take today. Board you can read today. But no slip leaves this counter without the sponsor's name beside yours." She turns the register flat and writes the name in a firm, quick hand — Alaric, no family line, the dash in the surname column filled with a short stroke like she's done it a hundred times. "Which brings us to the day's difficulty. Nobody in this hall volunteers. They'll want paying, or drinking, or both."

Hesta has stopped counting her coppers. She turns, looks Alaric over — bow, boots, the eyes — slow, like pricing a horse with a limp she can't find yet.

"Three coppers says he's bog-food inside a month," she says to Drem, not quietly.

"You don't have three coppers," Drem says. "You have my three coppers."

Hesta ignores him. Picks at the notched ear. "F-board's been rotting since Tuesday. Two vermin slips and a marsh-hag contract nobody F will touch. Ferran won't let me carry him on anything above vermin regardless — rules." A shrug that moves her whole shoulders. "Vermin I might sign. Might."

Ferran slides the oath form the last hand-width across the counter and sets the quill on it, crossways, deliberate.

"Oath first. Ink dries while you argue sponsorship."

Marsh-hag, eight silver, untouched by anyone with sense."

Hesta spits in her palm and holds the hand out flat, waiting, elbow locked — a hand that has closed on tusks and worse. Behind her, Drem shakes his head slowly at Alaric, a small, tired motion, the kind a man makes watching someone about to buy the same bad horse twice.

"Later?" Hesta's boot comes off the bench leg. "Boy, my third walks with you. Where you go, I go, till the ears are counted." She's at the desk before the slip is, snatching the quill out of Ferran's ink pot and scrawling her mark beside Alaric's name — a blunt G with a slash through it, signed the same way she'd gut something. "There. Inked. He goes alone, you don't pay out, right?"

"Contract is registered." Ferran blots it, files it, and pulls a second sheet for the day-log. "Rennick's yard, Limekiln Row — down river street, left at the cooper's, follow your nose the rest. Thirty copper on whole ears, he counts them himself, and he's been asking after his cellar four days running, so expect a welcome." The pen stops. "Lime pits eat leather. Mind the boots."

Limekiln Row announces itself two streets early. The smell rides in layers — burnt stone, dung vats, raw hide — and thickens the closer the river comes, until the houses give over entirely to long yards walled in flake-board, hides hung on wooden frames like laundry, gray side out. Apprentices stop to watch a stranger with a bow pass, then go back to scraping. An empty bark-cart rattles somewhere behind the walls.

Rennick's yard is the one with the gate off its latch and a man already standing in it, as if he'd been standing there a while. Heavy through the chest, forearms stained brown to the elbow, leather apron over a wool shirt gone stiff at the collar. A yellow dog sits behind his legs, ears up.

"Guild's, are you." He looks at the bow, then at Hesta, then back. "Four days I've had that slip up. Four days of them things chewing through my finished stock like it's after-meat." He steps back and waves them through the yard, past the pits — pale sludge, careful where anyone walks — to a low stone door in the yard's far corner, half cellar-door, half anything. It stands open on black steps going down. A sack of trimmings lies by the threshold, torn at one corner, spilling out.

"Third sack this week they've got at." Rennick crouches, puts the lantern he's carrying down on the top step, and doesn't open its shutter yet. His voice drops the way men talk about their own mistakes without meaning to. "They're not river rats. River rats run. These ones stand." The dog has come as far as the doorway and sits down there, hard, refusing the steps with its whole body. Rennick looks at the dog a moment, then at the dark. "Boy won't go past the top anymore. Used to sleep down there, winter nights."

Hesta pushes past, one boot on the second step, and looks back at Alaric over her shoulder, thumb hooked in her belt.

"Lantern's his. Blades are ours. You first, sponsored — I'm right behind you, and my third's watching how you work."

From down the steps, out of the black, comes a sound with no shape to it yet: small, many, and stopping all at once, as if something down there heard the light being discussed.

Claws first. The sound arrives before the shapes do — a skitter over greasy stone, and then the wedge of lantern light is full of bodies, low and fast, fur slicked dark.

The first set of teeth finds leather at the shin and digs in — a hot pinch through armor, not deep, but the weight of the thing yanking on the bootleg is enough to stagger a step. The big one comes off the heap's crown behind its pack, and it doesn't circle. It jumps, gets a claw-hold above the knee, and its bite closes on the meat of the thigh before it's thrown off — a second tear, wet through the padding, the whole left leg suddenly carrying its own heat.

"Move your feet, boy!" Hesta, from the light, not moving herself. "They're testing you. Kill one and the rest think twice!"

Rennick's voice behind her, tight: "Don't loose near my hides—"

The nearest rat — cat-heavy, jaws still working on the bootleg — is a hand's span from the arrowhead now. Behind it the pack is spreading wide, two peeling toward the stairs, cutting the retreat off at the knees. The big one has dropped back to four feet and is sitting on its haunches, licking blood off its own muzzle, watching. Learning.

The bowstring comes back to the ear. The ceiling takes the top limb — low, cramped, the draw just clearing the stone — and the point settles on the nearest rat's skull, its eyes already fixed on the arrow, not running, not yet.

The string goes.

Hesta's shout arrives late. The draw is already heavy in the fingers, full limb bent, the ceiling kissing the top of the fist, and the alpha is still sitting its haunches with its muzzle half-licked when the arrow takes it through the throat and pins the head back against the heap.

It doesn't scream. Rats don't. It folds the way a sack folds, and the heap under it drinks.

Then the floor comes alive again — not running from the kill, running through it. A body hits the torn thigh from the blind side, teeth finding the same wet seam as before, and the leg answers with a white flash of its own before the boot swings it off. The rest of the pack streams past on both sides now, close enough to feel the heat off them, and the two that cut toward the stairs stop short of the lantern wedge and sit there, blocking the bottom step, tails flat on the stone.

"HA! There's your winter firewood, Drem's coppers are MINE—" Hesta, at the top, all voice. Then, leaning over the light, dropping it: "But look at them, sponsored. Look. They're not breaking."

She's right. The pack has slowed. Spread. Not one has run for a wall. They circle at the edge of the reach of the bow, claws ticking on the greasy floor, and the taste of blood in the room is theirs now as much as anyone's.

Rennick, from above, quiet and sick: "Nineteen years I've run this yard. Never — they've never come at a man standing."

Overhead, boards creak. The yellow dog is barking now, up in the yard, and the sound comes down the stairwell thin and far away.

The arrows in the quiver: eighteen. The thigh is bleeding free under the leather. The pack is nine strong in the light and closing from three sides at once, and the alpha's body is already being — the word is too small for it — eaten. By its own.

"Next move's yours, boy! Fast one!"

The last rat takes the point through the chest mid-leap and lands already dead, sliding into the base of the spoil-heap. Then nothing. Claws stop ticking. Somewhere in the heap's tunnels, small things keep moving — things too far in to matter — but the light-wedge belongs to no one now except the dead.

Seventeen bodies, give or take the ones already half-eaten under the alpha. The big one hangs off the heap's crown with the first arrow still in its throat.

"HA!" Hesta takes the stairs two at a time, boots loud in the sudden quiet, and plants herself over the alpha's carcass like a flag. "Nineteen years, Rennick. Nineteen years that heap's been growing and the first man to clear it is a gate-fresh boy with red eyes. Drem's coppers are mine by supper." She crouches, grabs the alpha by the scruff, hefts it — heavy, both arms — and drops it. "Fat as pigs. All of them. What in Duskreach's name were you feeding this heap, the whole hide?"

"Trimmins. Fat scraps. What's left after the lime." Rennick has come down as far as the bottom step, lantern held high, and he is looking at his own cellar the way a man looks at a wound he dressed wrong. "Nineteen years it was a heap. This spring it started growing faster than I scrapes." He stops. Shuts his mouth on whatever came next.

Hesta is already working — knife out, one boot pinning the nearest carcass, cutting ears with quick, ugly efficiency. "You too, sponsored. Thirty copper's on ears, not on my knife-arm." She flicks the first pair onto the clean stone, then looks up, and the look stays on the leg. The left one. The leather there is dark and shining in the lantern light, and the shine is spreading.

"Sit down before you fall down. Rennick — cloth, water, something. He's leaking on your floor." Back to the ears, knife going, and her voice drops to the register she saves for things she means. "Bites go bad fast in a lime cellar. I've watched a man lose the whole leg to a rat smaller than these. You bind it tonight, boil the cloth if you've sense, and you don't pull another slip till it's closed. That's the sponsor talking, not the third."

Rennick has gone up for the cloth. Overhead the dog has stopped barking and started whining, thin and continuous, at the stairhead.

The quiver sits at seventeen. The heap still needs its nests torn out, Rennick will want it, and the ears are coming off the carcasses one pair at a time under Hesta's knife, wet clicks on stone.

"Count as you cut," she says. "Thirty copper means thirty pairs whole. He'll short us on anything ragged, and he'll be right to."

"Sixteen pair. Sixteen pair, whole as Sunday." Rennick counts the ears out on the top step twice, touching each one, lips moving. "Never thought I'd pay for rat ears smiling." The coins come out of an apron pocket already sorted into little paper twists, and he counts thirty copper into Alaric's palm without haggling — then pushes a strip of boiled cloth after it, gray and clean-smelling against the yard-stink. "For the leg. Wrap it tight, boy. Bites in a lime yard go sour faster than a hide in July."

He looks past them both, down at his cellar, at the heap with the alpha still pinned to it, and his voice drops to the register men use for things they don't want said twice.

"You'll not mention this around, the way they come at you. Standing. Nineteen years, and I'm telling you something in that heap changed." He stops there. Shuts the lantern shutter. Goes down the steps to his dead rats, and that's the last of him.

Hesta's arithmetic starts before the gate latch clicks. "Third of thirty's ten. You paid me ten for five days. So this one's square, sponsored — don't look so pleased, next slip I'm owed honest." She walks the whole way back counting her bet-money in advance, out loud, in coppers, while the Limekiln smell peels off street by street and river street opens up gray and busy under the morning.

The Guild hall hits like warmth and noise. Drem is exactly where he was, and his face when Hesta comes through the door is the face of a man who has already done the sums and hates each one.

"Three coppers," he says, before she's across the room. "Not a word out of you. Three." The coins go down on the counter one at a time, placed like funerals.

"Gate-fresh boy with red eyes cleared Rennick's cellar in under an hour!" Hesta announces it to the whole hall, both arms up, and the mail-cleaning women look over, and the sleeper on the bench surfaces just far enough to grumble and go back under. "Nineteen years that heap sat there. Nineteen! And a first-branch bowman—"

"Sit down, Hesta, the whole street heard you coming." Ferran has the ledger open before the slip crosses her counter. She reads it, blots the sponsor's mark, and writes one line in the day-log in that firm quick hand. "Contract closed. Rennick paid on delivery, so the desk's cut is nothing today. First contract inside a morning — that goes in the book, and the book doesn't care what I think of it." The pen taps the counter twice. She looks at the left leg, the dark shine gone stiff at the knee of the leather. "That binding wants salve under it by tonight. Dorn's shop, two streets over on Cooper's Lane, the provisioning one — she stocks a tallow-and-thyme that costs half what the herbalist charges and works twice. Tell her the desk sent you."

She files the slip and squares the drawer shut.

"Board clears at dusk. Hag slip reposts tomorrow, same eight silver, same nobody touching it." The pen goes back to the log. "You've a season before that one's your business. A season, mind. Not a week."

Hesta has stopped counting Drem's coppers. She's looking at the hag slip on the F-board, thumb hooked in her belt, and she doesn't say anything about it — but she doesn't sit down either.
